matches.text: <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> accounts of Joyce Jeffreys offer a rare opportunity to enter <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> social world of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> early modern spinster — her daily life, personal circumstances, social activities and family relationships are all reflected through <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> entries in her manuscript. <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> accounts also reveal extensive evidence of Joyce’s business dealings, most prominently as a moneylender in and around <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Hereford and Worcestershire region, but also as a farmer, market gardener, landholder, and horse and livestock dealer.

<IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> receipts section includes considerable detail about her loan arrangements and provides evidence of rental and other income. <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> disbursements section offers a wealth of information on contemporary expenses, including <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> cost of wages, food, drinks, clothing, textiles, medicines and medical care, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> training and care of horses, and even stud fees. Further entries relate to amounts paid out in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> form of gifts and gratuities, litigation fees, local and national assessments, and church dues.

Joyce Jeffreys appears at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> centre of a large, vibrant kinship network. Her business dealings extended beyond county boun- daries as far as London and she travelled regularly to visit relatives and friends, to listen to lectures, and to attend social events. Royalist by inclination, Joyce decided to abandon Hereford before <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> arrival of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Parliamentary army and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> social as well as economic costs of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> early civil wars are a further feature of her accounts.

Published in their entirety for <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> first time, these accounts reveal that Joyce Jeffreys was not as culturally or intellectually isolated as much of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> historiography of spinsterhood would have us believe.
Judith M. Spicksley is a Teaching Fellow in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Department of Economics and Related Studies at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> University of York.

As a learned society, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> British Academy seeks to sustain <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> health and promote <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> development of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> various academic disciplines that make up <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> humanities and social sciences. And as a grant-giving body, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> British Academy facilitates <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> research of individuals and groups of scholars.

<IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> series of Records of Social and Economic History includes some docu- ments which cover a large geographical area, even <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> whole country, as in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> recent volume of Diocesan Population Returns for 1563 and 1603. Some of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> documents that we publish, however, relate to a particular place and were produced by an individual. Such documents, which include accounts, journals and letters, are worthy of publication in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> series because they throw lights on <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> activities, practices or attitudes of a whole period or group of people. Personal account books are not very common in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> mid seventeenth century, so <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> book kept by Joyce Jeffreys is in itself a rare and valuable survival. It is, however, especially remarkable because it was kept by a woman, and extends beyond <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> household matters which we are accustomed to find, and reveals much about her business life. As well as making domestic purchases and paying servants’ wages, Joyce Jeffreys managed a farm, but devoted much of her capital to money lending. We have always known about <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> importance of credit in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> economy, before as well as during <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> period of industrialisation, but our information often consists of little more than <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> names of lenders and borrowers and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> sums owed in inventories or court cases. In this account book we can find out about <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> loans, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> creditors, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> interest payments, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> length of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> term and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> ultimate repayment of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> loan. Historians interested in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> credit market everywhere will find useful insights in these accounts, as will those also who work on such themes as religion and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> disruptions caused by <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Civil War. All of this is set in Hereford and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> villages around, which is a little studied part of England, but is revealed here as a complex society with its own special characteristics.

We are all grateful to Dr Spicksley who has devoted so much time and schol- arship to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> preparation of this text for publication. Because of her work Jeffreys can join that select band of seventeenth-century individuals—such as Loder, Josselyn and Pepys—whose personal writings tell us so much about <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> society and economy of that period.

Without <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> financial assistance of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Economic and Social Research Council of Great Britain, who granted me a three-year research fellowship in 2001, preparing this edition of Joyce Jeffreys’ accounts for publication would not have been possible. I am moreover, deeply indebted to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> British Library, for granting me permission to publish Joyce’s accounts and to Herefordshire Archive Service, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Bishop of Hereford, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> incumbent of All Saints’ Church, Hereford, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> unnamed depositor of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> document collection A63/VIII/I-138 and Worcester Record Office, for permission to publish extracts from manuscript documents in their possession.

Preparing Joyce’s accounts for publication has been an illuminating as well as an enjoyable experience, but it would have been much less pleasurable without <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> interest, support and encouragement of a great many individu- als. I have been repeatedly uplifted by <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> generosity of people both within and outside <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> field of history who have been willing to share with me their knowledge of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Hereford area in particular, and of early modern England more generally. I must especially thank Craig Muldrew, who read <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> entire manuscript and suggested a number of valuable improvements, but <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> fol- lowing people also made significant contributions at various stages in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> project: Charles Hopkinson; Beverly Lemire; Robert Tittler; Mandy Capern; and Mike Turner.

A special vote of thanks must also go to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Archivist and staff at Herefordshire Archive Service and at Worcester Record Office, who have fielded my numerous questions with speed and efficiency, and to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> staff at Hampton Court Estate, Hope under Dinmore, Herefordshire, who helped me uncover <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> history of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> house. My husband, Phil, took time off work to chauffeur me around Joyce’s numerous haunts, and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> photographs of Hampton Court and Ham Castle that appear in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> volume were taken by him.

For <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> opportunity to publish Joyce’s accounts, I am especially grateful to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> British Academy. Michael (F.M.L.) Thompson responded positively and with charm to an unknown writer, and Joanna Innes not only gave freely of her time and expertise, but also remained a patient and supportive supervisor to a publishing novice during what turned out to be a rather pro- tracted preparation process; Brigid Hamilton-Jones was immensely patient and helpful in finally bringing <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript to publication.
while I was employed on <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> ‘Perceptions of worth and social status in early modern England’ project. Her support and friendship have been invaluable.

I have discussed Joyce’s accounts with a great many people since work on this edition began, and their comments and insights have greatly improved <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> final result. Any mistakes that remain, however, are entirely my own.

Editorial Method and Commentary on <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Text

In setting out to edit Joyce’s accounts, I had two distinct aims in mind: to pre- serve as far as possible <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> look and feel of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> original document; yet at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> same time to make <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text comprehensible to as wide a range of readers as <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> material might interest. However, <IA_FTS_MATCH>finding</IA_FTS_MATCH> an appropriate balance between faithfully transcribing <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript and making <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text easily accessible has called for a considerable number of editorial decisions that will not delight every reader. In order to retain <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> look and feel of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> original man- uscript I decided at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> outset to adopt a tabularised system of editing, and keep <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> original spelling. Standardisation of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> English language was pro- ceeding hand in hand with an expansion in printing and a rise in literacy dur- ing <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> early modern period, but <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> pace was slow until <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> late seventeenth century.' Thus while there was less variation in seventeenth century letters and diaries than had been <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> case in their Elizabethan predecessors, consid- erable idiosyncrasy remained. Spelling was much less: uniform in private documents than in printed books and more especially in women’s writing.” In order to assist readers unfamiliar with early modern spelling practices to understand <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text, I have included with <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> glossary a brief discussion of Joyce’s most common orthographic forms. However, while I have retained <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> original spelling and layout of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript, my desire to improve <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> accessibility of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text has caused me to move beyond <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> more usual semi- diplomatic transcription and make <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> changes described in detail below. I have tried to compensate for this at least in part by incorporating a discussion of some of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> characteristics of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript—within <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> context of developments in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> English language—but students of early modern lin- guistics, and others with an especial interest in this area, are recommended to consult <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> British Library.

In editing <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript I decided in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> first instance to adopt a modern system of capitalisation, beginning each new entry with a capital letter, and introducing capitals at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> start of names, places and feast days. Occasionally <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> position a man occupied was included as part of his name, as in
'G. E. Dawson and L. Kennedy-Skipton, Elizabethan Handwriting 1500-1650: A Guide to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Reading of Documents and Manuscripts (London, 1966), 16.

‘Mr Maior, James Barroll’, for example, and in these circumstances I have capitalised <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> first letter of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> position as well as <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> name. <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> use of cap- ital letters often appears arbitrary in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> original text, although this can be explained to a large extent by reference to contemporary developments. Between 1593 and 1623 it seems that capitalisation was extended from its link at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> former date with certain categories of nouns only, to include any form of noun, adjective or verb by <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> latter.’ I have also replaced Joyce’s use of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> double lower case ‘ff’ at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> beginning of a word—employed to indicate a capital ‘F’—with <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> capital itself.

Secondly, though Joyce did add some punctuation to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript, I have re-punctuated <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> entire transcription, in order to make <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> entries in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> diary as unambiguous as possible. Five types of punctuation actually appear in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text: hyphens; colons; parentheses; commas; and periods or full stops. <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> latter three occur rarely, probably because <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript emerges as a set of accounts rather than a diary or correspondence, and there are no examples of semi-colons, despite <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> fact that they had been introduced between 1580 and 1590. But Joyce appears to have been particularly fond of colons. Prior to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> introduction of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> semi-colon, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> colon had been utilised to indicate a pause, but it was reinterpreted in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> sixteenth century to denote some logical progression or contrary information.* Joyce used colons in her writing for several stylistic purposes: in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> curtailment of fore- names for example; after numbers and dates; to represent a logical progres- sion; and to separate parts of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> entry. In addition, she occasionally replaced a colon with a dash or hypen, especially where pounds sterling were concerned.

Thirdly I have replaced <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> inter-changeability of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> characters u and v, and those of i and /, with <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> standard current modern uses of these letters (u and i as vowels and v and j as consonants). Originally u and v were differ- ent ways of writing <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> same letter, but in late Middle English it became <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> norm to use vy when it appeared at <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> beginning of a word and wu elsewhere. This was often <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> format adopted in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> printed literature of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, despite <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> fact that both wu and vy could rep- resent either a vowel or a consonant, and it was not until after 1630 that u and v were used phonetically.° Joyce adopted <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Middle English position insofar as she used v for all words beginning with either uv or v, but was less consis- tent about internal examples. <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> fact that she more commonly used v than u in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> middle of words when a consonant was required, however, is indica- tive of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> transitional status of her understanding during <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> period of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH>

manuscript’s construction. This situation is further reflected in her chrono- logical progression towards an increasingly fixed modern employment of these characters. However, Joyce did remain consistent in retaining <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> inter- changeability of iand/j. As in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> case of v and u, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> letter j had initially been a different form of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> letter 7. Through <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> sixteenth century many printers’ fonts included only <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> single capital form J, but by <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> second quarter of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> seventeenth century <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> use of i as a vowel and j as a consonant had entered writing practice in England.° Joyce’s continued use of i instead of j in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> late 1630s and 1640s suggests that <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> progress of this orthographic trend may not been have been as rapid as that of its uw and v counterpart, despite its adoption in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> printed literature; it must have occurred even later than Gorlach anticipated.’

Fourthly, for ease of reading I have expanded all abbreviations in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> body of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text in accordance with accepted conventions, except for a handful of well-known examples such as Mr, Mrs and etc.’ I have also retained rece as an abbreviation for received, since it occurs in practically every entry of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> receipt book. Joyce did not employ a bar or any other marks to indicate this contraction, although to be correct she should have done so (see below). And rather than use <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> standard abbreviation of an / crossed horizontally through (for <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Latin /ibra) to signify both <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> pound avoirdupois and <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> pound sterling as Joyce did, I have inserted /i for pounds sterling, and intro- duced /b for measures of weight to avoid confusion. Moreover, I decided to retain abbreviations contained within <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> marginalia in order to maintain as far as possible <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> original line format of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> manuscript, but only where <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> context is either clear from, or repeated in, <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> main body of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> text. Abbreviations in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> form of contractions, curtailments (or suspensions), brevigraphs and superscript were a common feature of writing during <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> early modern period, and Joyce’s manuscript is no exception. Most contrac- tions and curtailments were signalled by <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> appearance of a bar, known as a tittle or tilde, which in contractions was placed over <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> whole word in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> case of large omissions, or above <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> previous letter where only a single minis- cule, or lower case letter, was missing. In <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> case of curtailments <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> final e

was most often absent, but a bar over a vowel usually pointed to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> omission of an m or an n, as in fro (from) and upoé (upon), or of name endings, of which <IA_FTS_MATCH>Thé</IA_FTS_MATCH> for Thomas was <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> most frequent. Joyce also used another form of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> tittle, an upward and backward sloping curve from <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> last written miniscule, in writing abbreviated forms of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> months from September to December (which resulted in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> omission of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> final three letters—ber— from <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> month in question). In addition, she occasionally adopted <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> hori- zontal crossing through of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> double / to signal a missing e, rather than <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> tittle.

Like her contemporaries, Joyce adopted <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> use of certain brevigraphs or symbols in her writing. 4 <IA_FTS_MATCH>The</IA_FTS_MATCH> vicars choral existed in Hereford from at least 1237, when there were six vicars in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> cathedral church, two in full orders, two deacons and two sub deacons. By 1395 they were twenty-seven in num- ber—a custos and twenty-six vicars—with revenues, laws and a habitation, but they were unable to hold property. Richard II therefore granted them <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> form and title of Collegium vicarorium in choro ecclesie Herefordensis in 1395; they were to have a common seal and as a corporation were able to acquire and hold property. In <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> following century, however, problems of inclement weather and ‘evil doers’ reportedly made it difficult for them to go to church at midnight to celebrate divine service, and in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> 1470s they moved from their residence at 29 Castle Street to a new one situated to <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> east of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> Bishop’s Palace, in <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> cathedral precincts. During 1534 there were still twenty seven members of <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> college and under Elizabeth in 1583 a royal charter confirmed <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> vicars in their lands, possessions and rights as a corporation. But in 1637, under royal authority, a revised body of statutes was issued that fixed <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> number of vicars at twelve—with <IA_FTS_MATCH>the</IA_FTS_MATCH> possibility of a thirteenth—and four sub-canons.
